lead: Oregon's long rainy season, atmospheric rivers and mossy roofs drive most water damage. DryFlare helps owners from Portland to Eugene and Bend dry out properly.
risk: months of heavy rain, river flooding and roof and crawl space leaks
risk_short: heavy rain, river floods, roof leaks
why: Western Oregon gets most of its rain from October to April. Atmospheric rivers can drop days of heavy rain on soaked ground. The February 1996 flood put downtown Portland's seawall to the test and flooded towns across the Willamette Valley. Landslides on steep lots can push mud into homes.

Constant damp is the quiet problem. Moss holds water on roofs and lifts shingles. Many homes have crawl spaces that stay wet all winter. East of the Cascades, Bend and Klamath Falls see frozen pipes instead. Washington shares Oregon's wet winters, and Idaho shares the cold of the east side.
image_alt: Mold growing on a wall after a long-term leak
image_caption: Months of damp weather let mold grow on any wet wall in western Oregon.
problems: Roof leaks from moss and rain
Older homes in the Willamette Valley
tips: Clean moss off the roof and gutters every fall.
Keep a vapor barrier in the crawl space and check it each winter.
Run bathroom fans for 20 minutes after showers.
In Bend and eastern Oregon, insulate pipes before the first freeze.
insurance: Oregon policies often exclude damage from long-term leaks and rot, so fix roof and plumbing leaks as soon as you see them.

faq.q: Why is my Oregon crawl space always wet?
faq.a: Rain, high groundwater and poor drainage keep many Oregon crawl spaces damp. A torn vapor barrier or blocked drain makes it worse. Drying it out, fixing drainage and laying a new vapor barrier helps prevent mold and rot.
